title: Monaco GP 2026: Practice Sessions Analysis & Race Predictions
summary: Kimi Antonelli swept all three sectors to top our exclusive aggregated pace order at 1:12.610, but Ferrari's Leclerc and Hamilton are within striking distance and look devastatingly consistent. Using our combined-best-sector data, we break down who has truly nailed Monaco and who is leaving lap time on the table heading into qualifying.

sections.heading: The Headline: Antonelli's Statement Through Practice
sections.content:
Around the most unforgiving 3.337 km on the calendar, the smallest margins decide everything - and after three practice sessions our exclusive aggregated data points to a name that will worry the established order: Kimi Antonelli. The young Mercedes driver's combined-best-sector lap of 1:12.610, assembled entirely in FP3, was not just the fastest of the weekend; it was a clean sweep of all three sector bests, something no other driver managed.

But Monaco is rarely a one-team story, and the aggregated order tells a layered one. Charles Leclerc, roared on by the home crowd, sits second on a theoretical 1:12.833, just 0.223s back, while his Ferrari teammate Lewis Hamilton is third on 1:12.980. Max Verstappen (1:13.135) and George Russell (1:13.138) are separated by a barely-believable three thousandths, setting up a five-car fight for pole that is far tighter than the official single-lap timesheets suggest.

What makes this analysis different from anything on F1.com is the method. Our aggregated figures stitch together each driver's best individual sector across every session to reveal their ultimate, unexploited potential - the lap they could produce if they nailed all three sectors at once. On a circuit where a single locked brake into Sainte Dévote or a kissed barrier at the Swimming Pool ends a lap, that distinction between potential and delivery is the whole game.

The McLarens look like the weekend's biggest puzzle. Oscar Piastri sits sixth on aggregated pace (1:13.608) and Lando Norris eighth (1:13.751), with Norris in particular failing to string a representative lap together until FP3. For a team that has set the championship standard, a quiet Monaco practice raises real questions about whether the package suits low-speed, high-downforce demands.

sections.heading: Ultimate Pace Potential - Aggregated Order
sections.description: Each driver's combined best sectors across all practice sessions - exclusive data showing true potential beyond the official timesheets.

sections.heading: Sector-by-Sector: Where the Lap Is Won
sections.content:
Antonelli's pace is not built on one freakish sector - it is balanced across all three, which is exactly what makes it ominous. His 19.059s in Sector 1, 34.261s in Sector 2 and 19.290s in Sector 3 are each the fastest figures any driver recorded all weekend. When the same car owns the uphill blast to Casino, the technical descent to the tunnel, and the stop-start final third, the message is that the Mercedes simply works everywhere this track asks questions.

Ferrari's threat is concentrated in the middle sector. Hamilton's 34.365s and Leclerc's 34.386s in Sector 2 are the closest anyone gets to Antonelli, suggesting the Ferrari carries beautiful rotation through Mirabeau and the hairpin - traditionally where Monaco poles are decided. Leclerc edges the opening sector (19.112s) thanks to strong traction out of Sainte Dévote, while Hamilton claws time back in the final sector with a tidy 19.320s.

Verstappen and Russell expose the cost of an imperfect car balance. Verstappen's 19.195s opening sector is genuinely quick, but a 34.550s middle sector - nearly three tenths off Antonelli - is where Red Bull are losing this fight. Russell, by contrast, is rapid through the twisty bits (34.445s in S2) but drops time in the final sector (19.508s), hinting at a rear end that goes light over the kerbs at the Swimming Pool. Neither driver has a clean weakness; both have a single sector holding back an otherwise pole-worthy lap.

sections.heading: How to Read Aggregated vs Actual
sections.content:
Before the comparison table, it is worth being precise about what these two numbers mean, because they answer different questions. The aggregated lap is a theoretical optimum: it takes a driver's fastest Sector 1, fastest Sector 2 and fastest Sector 3 - potentially from three completely different laps - and adds them together. It represents the ceiling of what the car and driver have shown they can do.

The actual lap is the fastest single, complete lap a driver set, with all three sectors strung together cleanly. It is the number official sources publish, and it reflects consistency and real-world delivery under pressure. The gap between the two - the delta - is where the insight lives.

A small delta means a driver is already operating near their ceiling: they put the lap together when it mattered, which usually translates directly into qualifying performance. A large delta signals untapped time - a driver who has the raw pace in the car but has not yet assembled it into one lap. Because qualifying rewards exactly that ability to nail all three sectors at once, the aggregated order is the better predictor of Saturday, and the deltas tell you who still has margin to find.

sections.heading: How the Sessions Evolved
sections.content:
The story of the weekend is one of steady, dramatic track evolution - and of one team's late surge. In FP1, Ferrari set the early benchmark with Leclerc topping the aggregated order at 1:13.856 from Hamilton, the pair clearly comfortable on a green, dusty Friday surface. Antonelli was only fourth at that stage, half a second adrift.

FP2 saw the lap times tumble by roughly a full second as rubber went down, and Ferrari still held sway: Leclerc led on 1:12.884 from Hamilton, with Verstappen now third and a resurgent Russell fourth. Antonelli quietly moved up to fifth, but the more telling detail was Norris, who managed only nineteenth on aggregated pace after failing to complete representative low-fuel running - his best sectors stitched together from early laps.

Then came FP3, and the order rearranged. Antonelli unloaded the lap of the weekend, dropping to 1:12.610 and demoting both Ferraris. Leclerc and Hamilton remained within four tenths, but the momentum had shifted to Mercedes. Crucially, Norris and Piastri finally found their feet in the final session, climbing back to seventh and sixth respectively - evidence that McLaren's quiet weekend was as much about run-plan timing as a fundamental car deficit.

sections.heading: Tyre Strategy and Allocation
sections.content:
At a circuit where the race is so frequently decided on Saturday, the practice tyre picture is really a story about quoted preparation - how many fresh sets each driver banked for qualifying versus how many they burned chasing setup. The headline number belongs to Hamilton, who churned through 16 sets across the weekend, including a remarkable 11 softs - by far the most aggressive low-fuel programme of anyone, and a sign Ferrari were hunting for the last hundredths of single-lap pace.

McLaren mirrored each other almost exactly, Norris and Piastri each using 14 sets (eight soft, four medium, two hard), reflecting a methodical, data-gathering approach that may explain their slow build through the sessions. Verstappen sat in the middle on 13 sets, leaning heavily on the soft (ten used) as Red Bull searched for a balance that never quite arrived in the middle sector.

The more disciplined runners told a different tale. The Mercedes pair of Antonelli and Russell used just 11 sets each - efficient, targeted running that left them with five fresh softs apiece for qualifying. When a car is already fast, you do not need to thrash the tyres to find it, and Mercedes' restraint looks like a team that knew exactly what it had. Almost everyone at the front protected at least five soft sets for Saturday, with Hamilton and Hadjar squirrelling away six, underlining that on these streets, qualifying rubber is the currency that matters.

sections.heading: Key Findings and Surprises
sections.content:
Five things stand out once the data is laid bare.

1. Antonelli is the genuine pace-setter, not a timesheet fluke. Owning all three sector bests AND carrying only a 0.110s delta between aggregated and actual means he is both fast and already near his ceiling - the most dangerous combination heading into qualifying.

2. Hamilton is the consistency king. His +0.046s delta is the smallest in the entire field; whatever lap he shows you, he can repeat. On a circuit that punishes the slightest error, that reliability could outweigh raw potential.

3. Russell is the hidden threat. A +0.267s delta is the largest among the front-runners, meaning his 1:13.138 aggregated lap understates where he could land if he assembles it. Do not be surprised if he leaps up the order on Saturday.

4. McLaren's quiet weekend needs context. Norris's nineteenth in FP2 aggregated pace looks alarming until you see his run plan; the FP3 recovery and a +0.255s delta suggest there is a much better lap still in the car.

5. The midfield is desperately tight. Bortoleto (1:13.732), Norris, Hulkenberg (1:13.793) and Hadjar (1:13.813) are covered by less than a tenth on aggregated pace - a four-car scrap that could decide who sneaks into the top ten in qualifying.

sections.heading: Race Day Predictions
sections.content:
Qualifying Prediction: Basing this on the aggregated order - because on Saturday these drivers WILL nail all three sectors - pole is shaping up as a Mercedes-Ferrari duel. Antonelli's all-round command makes him the marginal favourite for a maiden Monaco pole, with a projected time in the 1:12.5–1:12.7 window if the track keeps improving. Leclerc and Hamilton are the obvious threats, and Russell is the wildcard who could gatecrash the front row given his untapped potential.

Predicted Top 3 (Qualifying): 1) Antonelli, 2) Leclerc, 3) Hamilton - with Verstappen and Russell breathing down their necks.

Race Prediction: This is Monaco, so qualifying position is destiny. Whoever starts on pole should convert, and track position will trump pace once the lights go out. If Antonelli delivers on Saturday, he is the favourite to win; if Ferrari lock out the front, Leclerc's home charge becomes almost unstoppable from the front.

Podium Prediction:
1. Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes)
2. Charles Leclerc (Ferrari)
3. Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari)

Wildcard Factors: A Monaco Safety Car is close to a statistical certainty, and the strategic gamble of pitting under it can flip the order entirely. Any threat of rain over the principality would scramble everything, particularly given no driver has banked meaningful wet-weather running.

Dark Horse: George Russell. The largest aggregated-to-actual delta among the front-runners means his real ceiling is higher than the timesheets show. If he strings it together when it counts, a front-row start - and a shot at the win - is firmly on.

Key Battle to Watch: The intra-Ferrari fight between Leclerc and Hamilton. Leclerc owns the first sector and the home crowd; Hamilton owns the consistency and the final sector. With nothing between them on aggregated pace, qualifying could come down to who survives traffic on their final run in Q3.
